narrationScript: Let's begin by understanding how to define a struct. You use the `struct` keyword, followed by a tag name—which, in our student example, would be 'Student'—and then a block enclosed in curly braces containing the declarations of its members. Each member is essentially a variable of a specific type. So, for our student, we might have a character array for the name, an integer for the ID, and a float for the GPA. This definition, importantly, doesn't allocate any memory. It's merely a blueprint, telling the C compiler what a 'Student' object will look like. Once you have this blueprint, you can declare actual variables of this new type, just like you would with an `int` or a `char`. For instance, `struct Student s1;` creates a variable named `s1` that conforms to our `Student` blueprint. To interact with the individual pieces of data within `s1`, we use the dot operator, a period. So, `s1.name` refers to the name member of `s1`, `s1.id` to the ID, and so on. You can assign values to these members, for example, using `strcpy` for strings or direct assignment for numbers. You can also initialize a struct variable directly when you declare it, using an initializer list with values matching the order of the members in the struct definition.
